ai.literal: Of right conduct those who renounced [their] greatness, as excellence, desires [to declare] the scriptures' conclusion.
ai.translation: The greatness of those who stand in right conduct and have renounced all desires is the supreme truth that scriptures desire to proclaim above all else.
ai.modern: ஒழுக்க நெறியில் நின்று ஆசைகளைத் துறந்தவர்களின் பெருமையையே, சிறந்ததாக நூல்களின் துணிவு போற்ற விரும்புகிறது.
ai.explanation: This couplet extols the greatness of those who have renounced worldly desires while firmly adhering to the path of righteous conduct. The word 'nīttār' refers to those who have renounced self-centered desires, while 'olukkam' emphasizes that their renunciation is rooted in moral discipline. The term 'panuval' refers to sacred texts or scriptures, and 'tuṇivu' means their ultimate, settled conclusion. The poet states that the ultimate consensus of all wise scriptures is to hold the greatness of these self-controlled ascetics as the highest virtue worth praising.

ai.literal: If one speaks of the measure of the greatness of those who have renounced, it is like counting all those who have died in the world.
ai.translation: To measure the greatness of those who have renounced all desires is like trying to count all the people who have ever died on this earth.
ai.modern: ஆசைகளைத் துறந்தவர்களுடைய பெருமையின் எல்லையைச் சொல்ல முயல்வது, இவ்வுலகத்தில் இதுவரை பிறந்து இறந்தவர்களை எண்ணிக் கணக்கிடுவதைப் போன்றது.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the infinite nature of the greatness of sages who have renounced worldly desires. The author uses a striking, impossible task as a comparison: counting every single person who has ever died on earth since the beginning of time. Just as it is impossible to keep a tally of all the deceased throughout human history, it is equally impossible to define or limit the spiritual stature of those who have conquered their desires. The key words 'துறந்தார்' (those who renounced) and 'பெருமை' (greatness) establish the subject, while 'இறந்தாரை எண்ணிக்கொண்டற்று' (like counting the dead) provides the vivid, hyperbolic analogy that emphasizes the boundless nature of their virtue.

ai.literal: The two-fold state's nature having understood, here virtue those who embraced, [their] greatness shone in the world.
ai.translation: The greatness of those who have understood the nature of both states of existence and have embraced virtue here in this world, shines supreme over the world.
ai.modern: பிறப்பு, வீடுபேறு ஆகிய இரண்டின் தன்மையையும் ஆராய்ந்து அறிந்து, இவ்வுலகில் அறநெறியை மேற்கொண்டவர்களின் பெருமையே உலகத்தில் உயர்ந்ததாக விளங்குகின்றது.
ai.explanation: This couplet praises the greatness of those who have renounced worldly desires. The word 'irumai' refers to the two-fold state of existence, representing the transient life of birth and the eternal state of liberation. By deeply analyzing and understanding the nature of these two states, wise sages choose to practice supreme virtue ('aṟam') while living in this world ('īṇṭu'). The poet emphasizes that the greatness of such individuals who have mastered this understanding shines as the most exalted thing in the world.

ai.literal: He who, with the elephant goad called willpower, controls all the five senses, is an excellent seed for the realm called the supreme state.
ai.translation: He who controls all five senses with the goad of willpower is a seed destined for the supreme realm of liberation.
ai.modern: மனவலிமை என்னும் அங்குசத்தைக் கொண்டு ஐந்து புலன்களையும் அடக்கிக் காப்பவன், வீடுபேறு என்னும் உயர் உலகிற்கு ஒரு சிறந்த விதையாவான்.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses the metaphor of elephant training to describe self-control. The five senses are like wild elephants that run amok, and 'uran' (willpower) is the sharp goad ('thotti') used to subdue them. A person who successfully restrains all five senses using this mental strength is praised as a 'seed' ('vithu'). This means they carry the potential and serve as the primary cause for reaching the supreme state of liberation ('varan').

ai.literal: The power of him who extinguished the five, the king of those in the wide heaven, Indra himself, is sufficient proof.
ai.translation: Indra, the king of the dwellers of the vast heavens, is himself sufficient proof of the great power of the one who has conquered all five senses.
ai.modern: ஐந்து புலன்களையும் அடக்கியவனுடைய ஆற்றலுக்கு, அகன்ற வானுலகில் வாழ்பவர்களின் தலைவனாகிய இந்திரனே போதுமான சான்றாவான்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the immense spiritual power of a person who has completely subdued their five senses. The poet uses the word 'அவித்தான்' (one who extinguished) to compare sensory desires to a raging fire that must be put out. To prove the magnitude of this achievement, the poet points to Indra, the king of the gods in the vast heavens, as a sufficient witness ('கரி'). Indra's own traditional stories serve as a testament to the consequences of failing to control the senses, thereby proving the supreme strength of those who successfully do so.

ai.literal: To do difficult things those who do are great people; small people are those who do not do things difficult to do.
ai.translation: Great are those who achieve deeds that are difficult to perform; those who cannot accomplish such difficult deeds are small.
ai.modern: செய்வதற்கு அரிய செயல்களைச் செய்பவர்கள் பெரியவர்கள்; செய்ய முடியாதவர்கள் சிறியவர்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts great individuals with lesser ones based on their capacity to perform difficult deeds. The author defines greatness not by birth or status, but by the ability to accomplish tasks that seem impossible to ordinary people. Those who shrink from difficult tasks and fail to perform them are deemed small or ordinary. The repetition of the phrase 'செயற்கு அரிய' (difficult to do) emphasizes that the true measure of a person's stature is the magnitude of the challenges they overcome.

ai.literal: Taste, sight, touch, sound, and smell—the world is within the grasp of the one who understands the nature of these five.
ai.translation: The world is within the grasp of the one who understands the true nature of the five senses: taste, sight, touch, hearing, and smell.
ai.modern: சுவை, ஒளி, தொடுதல், ஓசை, வாசனை ஆகிய ஐந்து புலன்களின் தன்மைகளை ஆராய்ந்து அறிபவனுடைய வசப்பட்டதே இவ்வுலகம்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the greatness of those who have mastered their sensory perceptions. The five senses—taste, sight, touch, hearing, and smell—are the primary channels through which human beings experience the material world. The poet states that the entire world lies within the understanding or control of the person who comprehends the true nature and workings of these five senses. By understanding how these senses operate and affect the mind, one transcends their limitations and gains true wisdom.

ai.literal: The greatness of the people of accomplished speech, on the earth, their hidden words will surely show.
ai.translation: The greatness of sages of accomplished speech is revealed to the world by their sublime, hidden words.
ai.modern: நிறைந்த ஆற்றல் உடைய சொற்களைப் பேசும் சான்றோர்களின் பெருமையை, அவர்கள் உலகிற்குத் தந்த மறைமொழிகளே (மந்திரங்களே) காட்டிவிடும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains how the greatness of realized sages who possess powerful, accomplished speech is made known to the world. Their 'hidden words', which refer to mantras or profound sacred utterances, serve as the ultimate proof of their spiritual stature. The power and truth of their words naturally reveal their greatness to everyone on earth without the need for external praise.

ai.literal: The anger of those who stood having climbed the hill called virtue, even for a moment, to withstand is difficult.
ai.translation: It is impossible to withstand, even for a single moment, the anger of those great ones who have ascended and stand upon the mountain of virtue.
ai.modern: நற்குணங்கள் என்னும் மலையின் மேல் ஏறி உயர்ந்து நிற்கும் பெரியோர்களின் கோபத்தை, ஒரு கணம் கூடத் தாங்குவது கடினமாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet describes the formidable power of the righteous anger of great sages. The metaphor of climbing a hill of virtue represents their lofty moral character and self-control. Although these realized souls are normally peaceful, if they do become angry, their wrath is so intense that it is impossible for anyone to withstand or survive its impact even for a single moment. Thus, the poet warns of the immense spiritual power possessed by those who have renounced worldly desires.

ai.literal: Those who are called Antanar are virtuous people, indeed, because of conducting themselves having assumed righteous compassion towards every living being.
ai.translation: They are called the truly virtuous who show righteous compassion to every living being and conduct their lives accordingly.
ai.modern: எல்லா உயிர்களிடத்தும் செம்மையான கருணையை மேற்கொண்டு வாழ்வதால், அறவோர்களே அந்தணர் என்று சொல்லப்படுபவர் ஆவர்.
ai.explanation: In this couplet, the poet defines true nobility and virtue based purely on ethical conduct and universal compassion. The key word 'sentanmai' combines righteousness and coolness, representing a gentle, loving-kindness. The poet asserts that true virtue belongs to those who assume this compassion and live by it toward all living creatures without exception. Thus, spiritual stature is defined not by birth or ritual, but by the active practice of benevolence.
